title: Page Tables & Translation
summary: The lookup structure hardware walks to turn a virtual address into a physical one, and why every real system makes it multi-level.

slides.markdown:
A **page table** is the lookup structure that maps a virtual page number to the physical frame number holding its actual data. Memory is managed in fixed-size chunks called **pages** (commonly 4KB) so the mapping stays a manageable size instead of tracking every individual byte.

A flat page table for a 64-bit address space would be absurdly large, so real systems build it as a **multi-level** tree instead — the design this Topic works through.

slides.subTitle: Virtual page number to physical frame number
slides.markdown:
A virtual address splits into two parts: a **virtual page number (VPN)** and a **page offset** (the byte position within the page). The page table maps each VPN to a **physical frame number (PFN)**; the offset is copied through unchanged since pages and frames are the same size.

So translation is really just: look up VPN in the page table, get back a PFN, then glue the unchanged offset onto it — the physical address is `(PFN, offset)`.

slides.subTitle: A flat table doesn't scale
slides.markdown:
A flat page table needs one entry per virtual page. With 4KB pages and a 64-bit address space, that's an astronomically large table — far more than any system could store, even though most processes only ever touch a tiny sliver of that address space.

A **multi-level (hierarchical)** page table fixes this by splitting the VPN into several smaller indices, each indexing into a level of a tree. Unused regions of the address space simply never get their lower-level tables allocated at all — the tree only grows where a process actually maps memory.

slides.subTitle: A multi-level walk, x86-64 style
slides.markdown:
x86-64 splits a virtual address into four page-table indices plus an offset, walking four levels before reaching the physical frame.

![A four-level page-table walk from a virtual address down to a physical frame, x86-64 style](assets/multi-level-page-table-walk.svg)

Each entry points to the next level's table, or — at the final level — the physical frame directly. A missing entry anywhere means that region was never mapped.

assets.alt: A four-level page-table walk from a virtual address down to a physical frame, x86-64 style

slides.subTitle: The page-table entry (PTE)
slides.markdown:
Each **page-table entry (PTE)** holds more than a frame number:

- **Frame number** — where the physical data lives.
- **Valid bit** — whether this entry points to a mapped page at all.
- **Protection bits** — read/write/execute, user/supervisor.
- **Dirty bit** — written since loaded (used by eviction).
- **Accessed bit** — referenced recently (approximates LRU).

Hardware checks every one of these on every access — a PTE is a small permission-and-bookkeeping record, not just a translation.

slides.subTitle: Splitting a virtual address
slides.markdown:
For a 32-bit virtual address with 4KB pages (12-bit offset) and a 2-level page table (10 bits per level):

```
Virtual address: 0x00403120
Binary:          0000 0000 0100 0000 0011 0001 0010 0000

Bits [31:22] -> level-1 index = 0x001  (10 bits)
Bits [21:12] -> level-2 index = 0x003  (10 bits)
Bits [11:0]  -> page offset   = 0x120  (12 bits, unchanged)
```

Each index selects one entry at its level; the final level-2 entry gives the physical frame number, which combines with the untouched offset to form the physical address.

slides.subTitle: Hierarchical vs inverted page tables
slides.markdown:
| | Hierarchical (per-process) | Inverted (one, system-wide) |
|---|---|---|
| Size scales with | Virtual address space used | Physical memory size |
| Lookup | Direct tree walk | Usually a hash lookup |
| Common in | x86, ARM, RISC-V | Some historical/PowerPC-family designs |

A hierarchical table's size only depends on how much of the (huge) virtual address space a process actually uses — sparse usage stays cheap. An inverted table has exactly one entry per physical frame system-wide, which caps its size by RAM (not address-space size) but needs a hash-based lookup instead of a direct walk, and is rarer in mainstream ISAs today.

slides.subTitle: Page tables aren't free
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Multi-level tables solve the space problem, so overhead is basically negligible."

**Why it's wrong:** a process touching memory sparsely across a huge range (ASLR, sparse data structures) can still force many intermediate tables to be allocated just to cover scattered pages — page-table metadata can become a real fraction of a process's footprint.

**Correct model:** multi-level tables cut worst-case overhead sharply versus a flat table, but don't eliminate it — page-table memory cost is a real, measurable concern.

slides.sectionTitle: Sizing the table: why flat doesn't scale
slides.markdown:
It's worth seeing the actual number that forces multi-level tables to exist. A flat, single-level page table for a 64-bit virtual address space with 4KB pages would need one entry per 4KB page across the *entire* addressable range:

```
2^64 bytes / 2^12 bytes-per-page = 2^52 entries
2^52 entries * 8 bytes/entry = 2^55 bytes ~ 36 petabytes
```

Even restricting to the actually-implemented 48-bit virtual address space of typical x86-64 systems, a flat table would need 2^36 entries — **512 GB** just to hold the table for one process's translations, dwarfing most machines' entire physical RAM. This is the concrete number behind "why multi-level": a multi-level tree only allocates the branches that cover actually-mapped regions, so a process using a few hundred MB of address space pays for a few hundred KB of page-table structure, not petabytes.
